title: Scale drawings, recipes and dosage proportions
blurb: Use proportions to read maps and blueprints, scale recipes up or down, and calculate liquid and tablet doses from the information given.
question: A medication order reads 0.375 g, and the bottle is labeled 250 mg per 5 mL. A map shows 1 inch = 25 miles, and a recipe for 8 servings needs 1 1/2 cups of milk. The TEAS asks how many mL to give, how far 3.5 inches is, and how much milk 12 servings need. What do these three problems have in common?

teach.body: Formally, a scale is the ratio of a length on a drawing or map to the actual length, a scale factor is the number you multiply by to resize, and a dose by proportion uses Desired ÷ Have × Quantity. In plain English: all three are proportions. A map, a recipe and a medication label each tell you one matching pair (1 in to 25 mi, 8 servings to 1 1/2 cups, 250 mg in 5 mL), and you scale that pair to the size you need.

items: Map scale 1 in = 25 mi. Two towns are 3.5 in apart: 3.5 × 25 = 87.5 miles. (Proportion: 1/25 = 3.5/x.)
Reverse: two cities 140 miles apart. 140 ÷ 25 = 5.6 inches on the map. Check: 5.6 × 25 = 140. ✓
Blueprint scale 1 cm : 2 m. A room 4.5 cm long on the plan is 4.5 × 2 = 9 m long.
Rule of thumb: drawing to real life, multiply by the scale; real life to drawing, divide by it.

teach.caption: When the scale's drawing side is not 1, divide by it first: 6 cm is three 2-cm units.

items: Scale factor = servings wanted ÷ servings in the recipe. Multiply EVERY ingredient by it.
3 cups of flour make 24 cookies. For 60 cookies: factor 60 ÷ 24 = 2.5, so 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 cups.
1 1/2 cups of milk serve 8. For 12 servings: factor 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5, so 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25 = 2 1/4 cups.
Check: 2.25 ÷ 12 = 0.1875 cup per serving and 1.5 ÷ 8 = 0.1875. ✓ Same amount per serving.

teach.body: A label gives a pair: a strength you HAVE (250 mg) in a QUANTITY (5 mL). The order gives the dose DESIRED. The amount to give is D ÷ H × Q. This is just the proportion 250/5 = 375/x solved in one line. Before you start, the desired dose and the dose on hand must be in the SAME unit, so convert grams to milligrams (× 1,000) first. On the TEAS every fact you need is in the stem: no nursing knowledge is required.

teach.h: Ordered 250 mg; label: 125 mg per 5 mL

steps.label: Sense-check
steps.sub: Twice the strength on hand, so twice 5 mL ✓

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs. Patel's liquid dose
items: Order: 0.375 g. Label: 250 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should be given?
Check with a proportion: 250/5 = 375/x gives 250x = 1,875, so x = 7.5 mL. ✓
Sense-check: 375 mg is a bit more than 250 mg, so the volume should be a bit more than 5 mL. ✓

teach.text: Three classic slips: flipping the fraction (Have ÷ Desired), skipping or botching the unit conversion (dividing 0.375 by 250, or turning 0.375 g into 37.5 mg), and using a LENGTH scale factor on an AREA. With a scale of 1 in : 4 ft, every length is × 4 but every area is × 16.

teach.h: Blueprint 1 in : 4 ft. Room drawn 2 in by 3 in
teach.caption: Safest method: convert each length to real size first, then calculate the area.

items: Maps and blueprints: drawing × scale = actual; actual ÷ scale = drawing.
Recipes: factor = new servings ÷ old servings; multiply every ingredient.
Dosage: Desired ÷ Have × Quantity, after converting to the same unit.
Areas scale by the square of the length factor: × 4 lengths means × 16 area.
Sense-check direction and size before choosing an answer.

summary: You can now use a scale to move between drawings and real distances, scale recipes with a single factor, and calculate liquid and tablet doses with Desired ÷ Have × Quantity after matching units. You can also avoid the area trap by converting lengths before finding area.

A.q: On a map, 1 inch represents 40 miles. Two towns are 2.75 inches apart on the map. What is the actual distance between them?

whyNot.0: 14.5 miles divides 40 by 2.75. Drawing to real life means multiplying by the scale.
whyNot.2: 42.75 miles adds 2.75 to 40 instead of multiplying.

A.q: A soup recipe that serves 6 uses 2.25 cups of broth. How much broth is needed to serve 10?

whyNot.0: 1.35 cups uses the factor upside down (6 ÷ 10), shrinking the recipe for more servings.
whyNot.1: 6.25 cups adds 4 cups for 4 more servings instead of scaling.
whyNot.2: 22.5 cups multiplies by 10 without dividing by the original 6 servings.

A.q: A provider orders 400 mg of a liquid medication. The label reads 100 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters should be given?

whyNot.1: 4 is D ÷ H; it still has to be multiplied by the 5-mL quantity.
whyNot.3: 80 mL divides the dose by the volume (400 ÷ 5) and ignores the strength.

B.q: A blueprint uses the scale 1 cm : 2.5 m. A hallway is 18 m long. How long is it on the blueprint?
B.why: Real life to drawing: divide by the scale. 18 ÷ 2.5 = 7.2 cm. Check: 7.2 × 2.5 = 18 m. ✓

whyNot.1: 45 cm multiplies by 2.5; going from real life to the drawing means dividing.
whyNot.2: 15.5 cm subtracts 2.5 from 18 instead of dividing.

B.q: An order calls for 0.25 g of a medication. Each tablet contains 125 mg. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.2: 20 tablets converts 0.25 g to 2,500 mg; grams to milligrams is × 1,000.
whyNot.3: 0.2 converts 0.25 g to 25 mg, moving the decimal only two places.

B.q: A scale drawing uses 1 inch : 5 feet. A patio is drawn 3 inches by 4 inches. What is the actual area of the patio?
B.why: Convert the lengths first: 3 × 5 = 15 ft and 4 × 5 = 20 ft. Area: 15 × 20 = 300 sq ft. (Drawing area 12 sq in × 5² = 300. ✓)

whyNot.0: 60 sq ft multiplies the drawing's area by 5; areas scale by 5 × 5 = 25.
whyNot.1: 12 is the area on the drawing, in square inches.
whyNot.3: 70 ft is the actual perimeter (2 × 15 + 2 × 20), not the area.

C.q: A medication is ordered at 15 mg per kg of body weight. A child weighs 44 lb. The liquid contains 100 mg per 5 mL. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milliliters should be given?
C.why: Weight: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. Dose: 15 × 20 = 300 mg. Volume: 300 ÷ 100 × 5 = 15 mL. Check: 15 mL holds 3 × 100 = 300 mg. ✓

whyNot.0: 33 mL uses 44 as kilograms (15 × 44 = 660 mg). Pounds must be converted first.
whyNot.2: 72.6 mL multiplies by 2.2 instead of dividing; pounds to kilograms makes the number smaller.
whyNot.3: 3 is D ÷ H (300 ÷ 100); it still has to be multiplied by 5 mL.

C.q: A 150-mL bottle of liquid medication contains 125 mg per 5 mL. The dose is 375 mg three times a day. For how many FULL days will the bottle last?
C.why: One dose: 375 ÷ 125 × 5 = 15 mL. Per day: 3 × 15 = 45 mL. 150 ÷ 45 = 3.33, so the bottle lasts 3 full days.

whyNot.1: 4 rounds 3.33 up, but there is not enough for a fourth full day (it needs 180 mL).
whyNot.2: 10 is the number of doses (150 ÷ 15), not the number of days.
whyNot.3: 3.3 is not a whole number of days; the question asks for full days.

C.q: On a map, 2 cm represents 15 km. Two clinics are 9.4 cm apart on the map. What is the actual distance between them?

whyNot.1: 141 km multiplies 9.4 by 15 but forgets that 15 km matches 2 cm, not 1 cm.
whyNot.2: 22.4 km adds the extra 7.4 cm to 15 km; scales multiply.

reteach.title: Ordering pizza for a study group
reteach.question: One large pizza feeds 3 people. Your study group grows from 6 to 15. How does the same thinking work for a recipe, a map and a medication label?

blocks.h: Find the multiplier, then multiply everything
blocks.body: 6 people need 2 pizzas. 15 people is 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5 times as many, so you need 2 × 2.5 = 5 pizzas. A recipe works the same way with cups instead of pizzas. A map works the same way with miles per inch. A medication label is 'one 5-mL spoon holds 125 mg', so a dose twice as big needs two spoons: 10 mL. Every problem is: find how many times bigger, then multiply.

blocks.text: The multiplier always compares the SAME kind of thing: people with people, mg with mg, cookies with cookies. Dividing mg by mL to get a 'multiplier' mixes units and gives a nonsense answer.

explain.body: The scale gives one matching pair. If 1/4 inch stands for 1 foot, each inch on the plan is 4 feet: divide the drawing length by 1/4 (or multiply by 4).

test.q: A floor plan uses the scale 1/4 inch = 1 foot. A wall measures 3 1/2 inches on the plan. How long is the actual wall?
test.why: Each 1/4 inch is 1 ft, so count the quarter-inches: 3.5 ÷ 0.25 = 14 ft. Check: 14 × 1/4 = 3.5 in. ✓

whyNot.0: 0.875 ft multiplies 3.5 by 1/4 instead of dividing.
whyNot.2: 7 ft treats the scale as 1/2 inch = 1 foot.

explain.body: Factor = servings wanted ÷ servings in the recipe. Multiply each ingredient by the same factor.

test.q: A recipe for 12 pancakes uses 1 1/2 cups of flour. How much flour is needed for 30 pancakes?
test.why: Factor: 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5. Flour: 1.5 × 2.5 = 3.75 cups. Check: 1.5 ÷ 12 = 0.125 and 3.75 ÷ 30 = 0.125 cup per pancake. ✓

whyNot.1: 0.6 cup uses the factor upside down (12 ÷ 30).
whyNot.2: 19.5 cups adds 18 cups for 18 more pancakes instead of scaling.
whyNot.3: 45 cups multiplies by 30 without dividing by the original 12.

explain.body: Divide the ordered dose by the strength on hand, then multiply by the volume (or tablet) that strength comes in.

test.q: A provider orders 75 mg of a medication. The vial is labeled 50 mg per 2 mL. How many milliliters should be drawn up? Round to the nearest hundredth if needed.

whyNot.1: 1.5 is D ÷ H; it still has to be multiplied by 2 mL.
whyNot.3: 37.5 mL divides the dose by the volume (75 ÷ 2).

explain.body: The order and the label must use the same unit before you divide. Grams to milligrams: multiply by 1,000 (1.2 g = 1,200 mg).

test.q: An order calls for 1.2 g of a medication. Tablets are 400 mg each. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.2: 30 tablets converts 1.2 g to 12,000 mg; grams to milligrams is × 1,000.
whyNot.3: 0.003 divides 1.2 by 400 without converting grams to milligrams.
